## 

![](images/clipboard-2133479479.png){width="100"}

**Goal** Does owning a smartphone influences sleep, depression, obesity?

## What we know - Linear Regression

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2+\dots+\epsilon, \qquad \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)
$$

- The [response]{.underline} is continuous (hours of sleep)

- The [predictors]{.underline} can be continuous of categorical (age, phone ownership, etc)

- The effects of the predictos act on the mean of the response.

. . .

**Example**

> If age uncreases by one year, keeping all other predictors constant, the mean slept hours decreases by $\beta$

## How do we estimate the parameters?{.smaller}

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(133)

# Simulate data
n <- 15
x <- seq(1, 10, length.out = n)
y <- 2 + 1.5 * x + rnorm(n, sd = 2)

df <- tibble(x, y)

# Fit linear regression
fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = df)

df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    yhat = predict(fit),
    residual = y - yhat
  )

# Create squares representing squared errors
squares <- map_dfr(1:nrow(df), function(i) {

  xi <- df$x[i]
  yi <- df$y[i]
  yhat <- df$yhat[i]

  side <- abs(yi - yhat)

  tibble(
    x = c(xi, xi + side, xi + side, xi),
    y = c(min(yi, yhat),
          min(yi, yhat),
          min(yi, yhat) + side,
          min(yi, yhat) + side),
    id = i
  )
})

# Compute MSE
mse <- mean(df$residual^2)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = x,
      xend = x,
      y = y,
      yend = yhat
    ),
    colour = "red",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = yhat),
    colour = "steelblue",
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = coef(fit)[1],
    slope = coef(fit)[2],
    colour = "steelblue",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

- We find the parameters that minimize the **loss function**:
$$
\sum_{i =1 }^n(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2 = \sum_{i =1 }^n(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i-\dots)^2
$$
- **Note** The model has strict assumption regarding parameters, linearity, independence

## The model {.smaller}

- We want the model to predict probabilities!

- We want a linear predictor of the form $\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots$

. . .

Let's try to fit a linear regression: $y =\beta_0 + \beta_1x +\epsilon$

```{r}
lm_fit  <- lm(y ~ hours, data = df)

glm_fit <- glm(
  y ~ hours,
  family = binomial,
  data = df
)

grid <- data.frame(
  hours = seq(0, 10, length.out = 200)
)

grid$lm_pred  <- predict(lm_fit, grid)


ggplot(df, aes(hours, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(hours, lm_pred,
        colour = "Linear regression"),
    linewidth = 1.2
  )  +  labs(
    y = "Probability of depression",
    colour = ""
  ) + xlab(" hours of smartphone use per day") + easy_remove_legend()
```

## Logistic Regression

We want to find a function of the probability to link to the linear predictor such that the predicted values always make sense!

. . .

```{r}

lm_fit  <- lm(y ~ hours, data = df)

glm_fit <- glm(
  y ~ hours,
  family = binomial,
  data = df
)

grid <- data.frame(
  hours = seq(0, 10, length.out = 200)
)

grid$lm_pred  <- predict(lm_fit, grid)
grid$glm_pred <- predict(glm_fit, grid,
                         type = "response")

ggplot(df, aes(hours, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(hours, lm_pred,
        colour = "Linear regression"),
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(hours, glm_pred,
        colour = "Logistic regression"),
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Linear regression" = "red",
      "Logistic regression" = "blue"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    y = "Probability of depression",
    colour = ""
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

## From probabilities to odds

> Odds are just another way to express probabilities!

Assume we have 100 childred, 20 sleep less than hours are 80 more.

- What is the probability that a randomly selected child sleeps less than 9 hours?

## From probabilities to odds{.smaller}

> Odds are just another way to express probabilities!

. . .

Assume we have 100 childred, 20 sleep less than hours are 80 more.

- What is the probability that a randomly selected child sleeps less than 9 hours? $\frac{20}{100} = 0.2$

. . .

- For every child who sleeps less than 9 hours, how many sleep at least 9 hours? $\frac{20}{80} = 0.25$

. . .

$$
\text{Odds} = \frac{\text{number of events}}{\text{number of non-events}} = \frac{p}{1-p}
$$

## Compute the odds

$$
\text{Odds} = \frac{\text{number of events}}{\text{number of non-events}} = \frac{p}{1-p}
$$


| Probability | Odds |
|-------------|------|
| 0.5         |      |
| 0.1         |      |
| 0.9         |      |


- What do odds equal to 4 mean?

## Compute the odds

| Probability | Odds |
|-------------|------|
| 0.5         |   1   |
| 0.1         |   0.111   |
| 0.9         |    9   |

- For each child sleeping less than 9 hours there are four   who sleep at least 9 hours.

## Odds and probability

```{r}
prob <- seq(0.01, 0.99, length.out = 200)

tibble(
  prob = prob,
  odds = prob/(1-prob)
) |>
ggplot(aes(prob, odds)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    x = "Probability",
    y = "Odds"
  )
```


## Log Odds and probability

```{r}
prob <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 200)

tibble(
  prob = prob,
  odds = log(prob/(1-prob))
) |>
ggplot(aes(prob, odds)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    x = "Probability",
    y = "log Odds"
  )
```






 
## Logistic regression

Logistic regression models log odds:

$$
\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\dots
$$

How do we interpret $\beta_1$?

A one-unit increase in $x$

- increases the **log odds** by $\beta_1$

. . .

Unfortunately, log-odds are not very intuitive.

## Parameter Interpretation{.smaller}


Instead, we exponentiate the coefficient

$$
OR = e^{\beta_1}
$$

where $OR$ is an **odds ratio**.

. . .

**Example: ** Suppose

$$
\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)
=
-3+0.4\times \text{Hours}
$$

Then

$$
OR=e^{0.4}=1.49
$$

. . .

**Interpretation**

For each additional hour of smartphone use,
the odds of sleeping less than 9 hours are multiplied by **1.49**
(approximately a **49% increase in odds**).


## Interpreting Odds Ratios{.smaller}

What do the following odds ratios mean?

| Odds Ratio | Interpretation |
|------------|---------------|
| 1.0 | ? |
| 1.3 | ? |
| 2.0 | ? |
| 0.7 | ? |

. . .


**Answers**

- OR = 1.0: no association
- OR = 1.3: odds are 30% higher
- OR = 2.0: odds are doubled
- OR = 0.7: odds are 30% lower

## Logistic regression as a prediction tool

We want to use logistic regression to predict (classify) new observation

 The model output is "probabilities" for example 
 
> The probability that a child using the mobile 6 hours a day sleeps less than 9 hours is 0.3

**Discussion**: How do you use this to predict if a child sleep less than 9 hours or not?

## Predicting with logistic regression

<!-- - prediction and classification -->
<!-- - model gives probabilities...how to you predciton? -->
<!-- - false positive false negative -->



```{r}

n <- 200

hours <- runif(n, 0, 10)
age   <- runif(n, 10, 15)

eta <- -17 +
  0.8 * hours +
  0.9 * age +
  0.25 * (hours - 5) * (age - 12.5)

p <- plogis(eta)

y <- rbinom(n, 1, p)

df <- tibble(
  hours,
  age,
  y
)

log_fit <- glm(
  y ~ hours + age,
  family = binomial,
  data = df
)

preds = data.frame(df, pred_p = predict(log_fit, df, type = "response")) %>%
  mutate(pp = ifelse(pred_p>0.5,1,0))


grid <- expand.grid(
  hours = seq(min(df$hours),
              max(df$hours),
              length.out = 200),
  age   = seq(min(df$age),
              max(df$age),
              length.out = 200)
)

grid$prob_logit <- predict(
  log_fit,
  newdata = grid,
  type = "response"
)



grid_long <- bind_rows(
  grid %>%
    transmute(
      hours,
      age,
      prob = prob_logit,
      model = "Logistic regression"
    )
)


ggplot() +

  geom_raster(
    data = grid_long,
    aes(hours, age, fill = prob),
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +

  geom_contour(
    data = grid_long,
    aes(hours, age, z = prob),
    breaks = 0.5,
    colour = "black",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +

  geom_point(
    data = df,
    aes(hours, age, colour = factor(y)),
    alpha = .6,
    size = 1.5
  ) +

  facet_wrap(~model) +

  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "Predicted\nProbability"
  ) +

  labs(
    x = "Hours smartphone use",
    y = "Age",
    colour = "Observed"
  ) +

  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)



```







## Predicting with logistic regression

<!-- - prediction and classification -->
<!-- - model gives probabilities...how to you predciton? -->
<!-- - false positive false negative -->



```{r}




preds = data.frame(df, pred_p = predict(log_fit, df, type = "response")) %>%
  mutate(pp = ifelse(pred_p>0.5,1,0))


grid <- expand.grid(
  hours = seq(min(df$hours),
              max(df$hours),
              length.out = 200),
  age   = seq(min(df$age),
              max(df$age),
              length.out = 200)
)

grid$prob_logit <- predict(
  log_fit,
  newdata = grid,
  type = "response"
)



grid_long <- bind_rows(
  grid %>%
    transmute(
      hours,
      age,
      prob = prob_logit,
      model = "Logistic regression"
    )
)


ggplot() +

  geom_raster(
    data = grid_long,
    aes(hours, age, fill = prob),
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +

  geom_contour(
    data = grid_long,
    aes(hours, age, z = prob),
    breaks = 0.5,
    colour = "black",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +

  geom_point(
    data = df,
    aes(hours, age, colour = factor(y)),
    alpha = .6,
    size = 1.5
  ) +

  facet_wrap(~model) +

  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "Predicted\nProbability"
  ) +

  labs(
    x = "Hours smartphone use",
    y = "Age",
    colour = "Observed"
  ) +
  geom_point(data = preds %>% filter(y==1, pp==0),
             aes(hours, age), shape = 21
             ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)



```
False Negative: predicted to be 0, observed to be 1

## Linear and logistic regression{.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Linear Regression
$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \epsilon
$$

- Response is continuous

- Covariates act linearly on the mean

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

Logistic Regression
$$
\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x 
$$

- Response is binary (0/1)
- Covariates act linearly on the odds
:::
:::::

. . .

What they have in common:

- Clear model assumptions
- Simple and rigid relation between covariates and response
- Few parameters ( #covariates $\ll$ #observations)
- The parameters are interpretable
